statement: Which capital letter, printed plainly, has both a horizontal and a vertical line of symmetry?

choices.misconception: I found the vertical fold and assumed a horizontal one must work too.
I found the horizontal fold and stopped without testing the vertical one.
I counted the vertical fold twice rather than testing a horizontal one.
I mistook turning the letter upside down for folding it, which is rotation rather than symmetry about a line.

hints: Fold each letter twice: across, then down.
Test both folds separately on every letter. A letter passes only if the two halves land exactly on each other for the horizontal fold and for the vertical fold.
A and T fold vertically only. B folds horizontally only. Z looks the same upside down but has no fold at all. H folds both ways.

solutions.reliable: Test both folds on each letter. A folds along a vertical line but not a horizontal one. B folds horizontally but not vertically. T folds vertically only. Z has no line of symmetry at all - it looks the same when turned half a turn, which is rotation, not reflection. H folds along both its vertical and its horizontal midline. The transferable idea: looking the same after a turn is not the same as having a line of symmetry, and choice E is exactly that confusion.

whyOnTest: Confusing rotational symmetry with a line of symmetry is a distinct, common error, and Z is the letter that exposes it.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
